A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same research work. Their text, equations, figures, and complete appendices are readable, and retained algorithms and proofs can be matched across renumbering and relocation.

before.justification: v1 reports theoretical results and proofs, without original empirical outcomes. Figure 1 illustrates the potential function rather than an experiment.

after.justification: Section 5 reports original simulations on four synthetic instance families and finite adversarial counterexamples. Figure 2 presents fairness and welfare results with confidence intervals.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 and the existing one-sided-error adaptation are retained. However, v2 adds preprocessing for bounded two-sided prediction errors: inflate predictions by 1/(1-rho), then apply the one-sided guarantee with epsilon = 2rho/(1+rho) (Section 5, footnote 7).

E1.justification: v1 has no empirical evaluation. v2 evaluates online allocation on four synthetic valuation families: uniform, dense binary-interest, correlated, and specialist instances. It also empirically tests adversarial sequences derived from the existing greedy counterexamples.

E2.justification: v2 introduces numerical comparisons of Algorithm 1 against Greedy-1, Greedy-2, and Greedy-3 in Section 5 and Figure 2. These strategies were defined and analyzed theoretically in v1, but were not empirically evaluated against Algorithm 1.

E3.justification: The new random-instance evaluation uses eight agents, forty goods, per-agent maximum-value normalization, realized PROP1 ratios, and utilitarian welfare normalized by the ex-post optimum. Separate adversarial tests use prefixes of roughly 500 goods. These are newly introduced protocols, not revisions to earlier experiments.

E4.justification: v2 adds focused stress tests of the three existing counterexample constructions, checking their finite-prefix effects on greedy fairness and comparing Algorithm 1 on the same prefixes. v1 provides only the mathematical constructions and proofs.

E5.justification: v2 introduces repeated-trial and uncertainty reporting throughout its new random-instance evaluation: 500 independent trials per family and 95% confidence intervals in Figure 2. v1 contains no empirical run counts or confidence intervals; this is not an increase from a previously reported run budget.

E6.justification: v2 adds the first empirical scores, reporting that Algorithm 1 achieves PROP1 on every sampled random instance. For example, on dense instances its welfare is 0.960 versus Greedy-1's 0.954, with PROP1 ratios 1 versus 0.423. New adversarial results also quantify greedy failures and Algorithm 1's performance.

T1.justification: v2 adds a matching limitation for RAND (Proposition 4.2) and a near-proportionality guarantee under a small-item condition (Theorem 4.3), with proofs in Appendix C. It also repairs greedy proof steps, changes the concentration-proof constant from 27/(128 log(n/delta)) to 3/(32 log(n/delta)), and corrects the displayed potential to match the retained algorithm.

C1.justification: Section 1.1 expands the random-allocation contribution from a logarithmic approximation guarantee to an essentially tight characterization for RAND, plus near-proportionality under small items. The principal greedy-impossibility and MIV-assisted 1/n-PROP1 claims remain.

C2.justification: v2 adds substantive interpretations of empirical fairness-welfare tradeoffs and benign versus adversarial instances. It also explains why MIV information obstructs standard lower-bound constructions and explicitly limits the new tightness result to RAND, leaving stronger general online algorithms possible.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-repository link in Section 5, footnote 8, and synthetic-data generation details, including interest probability 0.6, positive values in [0.8, 1], and the correlated-value formula. v1 already supplies the core pseudocode and proofs but no implementation link.

R1.justification: v2 adds references supporting the greedy strategies, including Plaut and Roughgarden (2018), and expands background coverage of online voting and learning-augmented algorithms. Some earlier EFX and temporal-fair-division references are removed. The central relationship to Neoh et al. (2025) and Zhou et al. (2023) remains.

P1.justification: The introduction and contribution narrative are extensively rewritten around machine-learning allocation systems. General related-work material moves to a new Appendix A, the conclusion is rewritten, and the greedy proof sketch and potential-function explanation are substantially revised.

P2.justification: The main text changes from a single-column manuscript to a two-column conference layout with running headers and a full-width algorithm display. The unchanged Figure 1 is relocated and resized, while new Figure 2 introduces four fairness-welfare panels with legends and confidence intervals.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens theoretical completeness and reliability by establishing RAND's tightness and small-item regime while correcting proof and formula errors in v1. The new simulations, confidence intervals, and adversarial stress tests provide useful evidence about fairness-welfare behavior that the theoretical guarantees alone do not establish. Although the empirical support remains limited to synthetic settings, the combined gains are substantial.
